newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - GKN boosts profits, sees more growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - GKN boosts profits, sees more growth.

text.p: International engineering group GKN Plc unveiled a 12.2 percent rise in half-year profits on Wednesday, beating market forecasts and sending the share price soaring.
The share rose 75p to 11.61 pounds, adding over 250 million pounds to the company's market value.
Analysts said current year forecasts of around 385 million pounds pre-tax were likely to be raised to 400 million pounds, up from last year's 362.8 million.
Pre-tax profits for the six months to June 28 rose to 203 million pounds, against 181 million last year and topping forecasts of between 185 and 193 million pounds.

Sales were down 2.3 percent at 1.69 billion pounds, but the firm said sterling's strength in translating results belied stronger underlying growth which would have shown a 25 percent jump in profits and six percent rise in sales at constant exchange rates.

"All our major businesses delivered very strong performances in the first six months of 1997. This progress has been achieved despite the impact of currency translation rates," chief executive CK Chow said.
Chow said he felt confident with the underlying strength of businesses that "1997 should be another year of growth for GKN."

The balance sheet was strong and cash balances of 247 million pounds after spending 356 million pounds on acquisitions in the first-half placed the group in a good position "to fund further strategic development."

Profits in the automotive products division were up five million pounds at 106 million pounds, on sales of 1.02 billion pounds while profits in the aerospace and defence vehicles division jumped 13 million to 51 million pounds on sales of 460 million.
The industrial services division which centres on the Chep
distribution pallets and crates hire business, increased profits by five million to 42 million pounds on sales of 208 million pounds.
"The numbers looked very good," said Andy Chambers, London-based industry analyst with SocGen. "The aerospace division has done much better than expected," he added.
Chow told Reuters in an interview he saw plenty of scope for growth from all areas, including its traditional mainstay, the vehicle driveshaft business.
Despite the maturity of European and North American vehicle markets and GKN's leading market share, the company believed there was still rich potential for growth in the driveline business, he said.
GKN was taking new supply contracts as vehicle manufacturers decided to outsource more components and it was also moving in on emerging markets, particularly in China and Mexico.
"It is our aim to triple our business in emerging markets in the next five years," Chow said.

A strategic review of the group undertaken since he took over the reins in January had identified three areas of organic growth and a further three "platforms for growth" following recent acquisitions, he told Reuters.

Organic growth was seen coming from the driveshaft business, from Chep and from Westland Helicopters, while acquisitions had laid the foundations for further growth in automotive and aerospace components manufacture.
In particular GKN's business making vehicle components by moulding powdered metals was set to take off following its takeover of U.S. firm Sinter Metals for $570 million in May.
Now GKN was on the lookout for further acquisitions, but declined to comment on recent speculation GKN might have its eye on British rival T&N.
"The sector is growing at six to 10 percent a year and we believe we can grow faster than that because we can play the consolidator role," he said.

Chow said he had identified a second platform for growth in automotive components in GKN's 'Agritechnical' business supplying off-road vehicle components, which led to the acquisition of a 39 percent stake in Italian firm, Agrindustrial Holdings, in March.
In aerospace and defence, Chow said helicopter production at its Westland unit would jump as it delivers on an order book currently worth 3.8 billion pounds.
Annual production rates are due to rise from nine helicopters in 1997 and 1998 to 42 in 2000, he said.

Meanwhile GKN Westland Aerospace, which makes substructures for other aircraft manufacturers, was enjoying strong organic growth from the recent industry upturn. Chow said he now saw this unit as his third platform for growth, having added three more acquisitions to the business in the first half of this year.
